newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto woes may mean swift new Japan election.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto woes may mean swift new Japan election.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, paying the price for wounding but not knocking out his opposition, is looking at a bleak future that could include another general election within a year.
One week after a general election that took Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) tantalisingly close to a parliamentary majority, the prime minister finds himself suddenly on the defensive.
His search for coalition partners, and even defectors from other parties, is coming up empty as politicians realise another election may be the only way out for Hashimoto.
With about 10 days left until parliament is expected to reconvene, most bets are on Hashimoto going into the session at the head of a minority government of just his LDP.

"However, without a majority of seats in the Lower House, the LDP would constantly face the possibility of losing a vote on a no-confidence motion...and that situation would make his government an unstable one," the Asahi Shimbun said in a front-page story on Monday.
Political analysts' forecasts of a date of a snap poll range from as early as next January to this time next year.

In the October 20 poll, the LDP won 28 more seats to take it to 239 in the 500-seat parliament -- too few to govern alone and too many for its old coalition partners, the Social Democrats and the Sakigake party, to feel comfortable about continuing an alliance.
The Social Democrats fell from 30 to 15 seats and Sakigake, an LDP splinter group, from nine to two.
"We campaigned on keeping the current coalition, and the result means our position was dealt a definite 'no'," Sakigake leader Shoichi Ide said.
"The lesson is that small parties get swallowed by big ones in a coalition and the electorate says, 'Why should we vote for you at all?'" Ide himself lost his seat.
Fearful that a new alliance with the LDP would weaken them even further in the next election, both the Social Democrats and Sakigake are so far keeping the LDP at bay.

Complicating Hashimoto's search even more is the LDP's conservative wing, which believes that the party's electoral gains mean there is less need to compromise on policies to bring possible coalition partners into the fold.

Seeing Hashimoto's dilemma, and how it could lead to a swift new election, the country's two biggest opposition parties have bound up their wounds -- at least publicly -- and shown a new sense of unity.
Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), the biggest opposition group, settled a leadership row which threatened to split the party in the days after the election, retaining Ichiro Ozawa as its chief.
Some members of the Democratic Party, the second-biggest opposition group, briefly flirted with the idea of joining an LDP-led coalition but this possibility now seems dead.
The party was formed just one month ago, mainly by defectors from the junior coalition partners who already saw the writing on the wall about the demise of their parties.
"It is almost certain that the Democratic Party will not join the ruling camp," co-leader Health Minister Naoto Kan said on Sunday.
The respected weekly news magazine, Aera, looking at Hashimoto's problems, forecast on Monday that a new election could be called as early as next January.

"If the LDP ends up as a minority government there could be a rematch general election as early as January after drafting of the budget, or if not then, next May after the budget is passed," the magazine said in its latest edition.
Political commentator Makoto Sakata refused to make a prediction about the date of a new election.
"But the LDP does not have a bright future," he told Reuters.
